note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: SEE the actual same-species flowering panicles in panels 1,3,9–10 (indices 0,2,8,9). Ozarkgrass is an annual with a usually narrow, sometimes nodding spring panicle and one-flowered spikelets; only the published key—not these images—establishes two near-equal glumes, the apical lemma teeth and single awn between them. Do not use lovegrass/threeawn comparison photographs as though they were Ozarkgrass.
tiles.short: Narrow spring panicle; one-flowered spikelet with one bent awn
tiles.status: FIELD-READY SPRING PANICLE AND AWN CUE — SINGLE LEMMA-NOTCH MACRO MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · TRACE THE ANNUAL BASE
tiles.details: Field habitat in panel 1 (index 0) shows green leafy shoots at the soil surface, NOT any exposed roots. Bob Harms' habit plate in panel 9 (index 8) includes a small basal root strand at the bottom of a separated left-hand culm; the central flowering panicle is on a different cut/laid stem. That does NOT prove an intact same-plant fibrous root crown plus flowering culm. To clear the gate, photograph one legally collected rooted individual upright in place, then dug with entire connected root system/crown/flowering head and a centimeter scale.
tiles.short: Fibrous-rooted annual; panicle to ~12 cm in local treatment
tiles.status: PARTIAL SEPARATE BASAL ROOT STRAND — CONNECTED ROOT-TO-FLOWERING PLANT STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1282) — Look inside the blade–sheath junction for a short membrane with a ragged, fringed edge. The Flora gives 1–2 mm.

Actual exact-species blade–sheath junction photos are panel 4, Chet Burrier's full-size macro (index 3), and panel 14, Bob Harms' regional collar view (index 13). The Chet image shows pale projecting torn/ragged-looking junction tissue, not a fully opened inner membrane beside a millimeter bar. The Harms plate shows a photographed collar region, but no continuous clearly calibrated free ligule edge. Texas Hill Country key describes a 1–2 mm membranous, obtuse, lacerate ligule, glabrous collar, no auricles. Photograph the adaxial/INNER free edge with a ruler before claiming the length.

Photo still needed: an inner view with the free ligule edge in focus beside a millimeter scale.
tiles.short: Membranous 1–2 mm; truncate and finely jagged
tiles.status: TWO REAL COLLAR PHOTOS — MEASURED INNER LIGULE STILL NEEDED

tiles.heading: 04 · COUNT AND MEASURE GLUMES
tiles.details:
Panels 2 and 11–12 (indices 1,10,11) show authentic Ozarkgrass awned flowering material. Neither proves both 3–5-veined glumes are separated and measured. The Williamson County treatment reports roughly 3–3.3 mm glumes; Kew GrassBase gives ~3.5–4 mm spikelets with one fertile floret and a barren rachilla extension. These are source measurements, NOT numbers derived from the images. Do not point glume arrows at uncertain scales in a cramped old source plate.

Photo still needed: one mature spikelet with both glumes visible beside a millimeter scale.

Compare attached and isolated awned units. A separated glume pair and a millimeter scale are still needed.
tiles.short: Two subequal awnless glumes, ~3–3.3 mm locally
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — TWO MEASURED GLUMES AND ONE FLORET

tiles.heading: 05 · FIND THE TWO-TOOTHED LEMMA
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1282) — Turn the lemma so you can see its back. The Flora describes a single bent awn arising at or near the base of the two small tip teeth.

Actual Limnodea awns appear in panels 2,5 and 11–12 (indices 1,4,10,11). Critical identification: the ONE awn emerges between TWO small teeth on a fertile lemma, not from a glume. Existing full-size photos do not isolate the two ~0.5-mm teeth at 20–40× with a mm reference, so gross awn arrows are okay but new tooth/awn-origin markers remain prohibited.

These views show the awns on intact spikelets. Photo still needed: an isolated lemma turned so the two teeth and the awn’s attachment are visible together.
tiles.short: Lemma 2.7–2.9 mm; one 8–12.5 mm awn BETWEEN two teeth
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — LEMMA TEETH AND AWN INSERTION

tiles.heading: 06 · RULE OUT THREEAWNS AND LOVEGRASSES
tiles.details: Three look-alike gallery panels are numbered 6,7,8 (indices 5,6,7): Aristida purpurea, Panicum virgatum and Eragrostis intermedia, respectively. None is a photograph of Limnodea. The Ozarkgrass reproductive comparison is panel 12 (index 11); one long awn alone is insufficient, because some Muhlenbergia also bear one. Confirm two-toothed lemma and glumes rather than confusing grass seeds or species images. Keep Joey Santore's individually licensed iNaturalist lovegrass photo on conditional NC terms only.
tiles.short: One notched-lemma awn ≠ Aristida's three awn limbs
tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE LESSON; MATCHED DISSECTED COMPARISONS MISSING

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: OZARKGRASS: find a slender annual tuft with fibrous roots and a relatively NARROW, sometimes slightly nodding spring panicle. At 10–20× inspect ONE ~3–4 mm spikelet: TWO stiff nearly equal glumes enclose ONE fertile floret. The lemma has TWO small apical teeth; its SINGLE 8–12 mm often bent and twisted awn emerges BETWEEN those teeth. A true 1–2 mm membranous, minutely jagged ligule sits inside the blade–sheath junction. Flowerhead silhouette alone is not a confirmed ID; the current photo does NOT prove lemma teeth or ligule.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Species panels 1,3 and 9–10 show clump and narrow panicles. The Harms plate panel 9 (index 8) includes a separate root strand but lacks a fully connected flowering specimen; the CC0 field tuft panel 1 (index 0) does not expose roots.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Field habitat in panel 1 (index 0) shows green leafy shoots at the soil surface, NOT any exposed roots. Bob Harms' habit plate in panel 9 (index 8) includes a small basal root strand at the bottom of a separated left-hand culm; the central flowering panicle is on a different cut/laid stem. That does NOT prove an intact same-plant fibrous root crown plus flowering culm. To clear the gate, photograph one legally collected rooted individual upright in place, then dug with entire connected root system/crown/flowering head and a centimeter scale.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Panels 2 and 11–12 (indices 1,10,11) show authentic Ozarkgrass awned flowering material. Neither proves both 3–5-veined glumes are separated and measured. The Williamson County treatment reports roughly 3–3.3 mm glumes; Kew GrassBase gives ~3.5–4 mm spikelets with one fertile floret and a barren rachilla extension. These are source measurements, NOT numbers derived from the images. Do not point glume arrows at uncertain scales in a cramped old source plate.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Aristida threeawns: normally THREE awn limbs arising from ONE lemma, vs Limnodea's single notched-lemma awn. Eragrostis lovegrasses: generally MULTIPLE florets per spikelet, not just one. Panicum (e.g., switchgrass): typically a lower sterile/staminate floret with a hardened fertile UPPER floret rather than one fertile floret with the Limnodea notched awn. Muhlenbergia: can ALSO have one fertile floret, so compare the paired glumes, lemma teeth/awn origin, ligule and annual tuft; panicle openness and one awn alone are insufficient.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

memory_rule: One fertile floret + 2 long nearly equal stiff glumes + 2 lemma-tip teeth framing ONE bent awn = Ozarkgrass candidate. Count actual florets and inspect the awn attachment.
safety_note: These photos teach recognition, not a Hays County native-range certification; final site rights-filtered deployment and mobile arrow QA are still unverified.
field_rule: NEVER certify a root-to-panicle connection, true ligule measurement, or 0.5 mm paired lemma teeth from photographs that do not show those structures plainly.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
